summary: A running C program's memory is split into segments: text, initialized data, BSS, heap, and stack. Knowing which variable lands where explains lifetimes, crashes, and security bugs.

sections.heading: The big picture
sections.body: From low to high addresses: text, initialized data, BSS, heap (grows up), a large gap, then the stack (grows down). When the two growing regions collide, memory is exhausted. Exact placement is randomized on modern systems (ASLR) but the ordering idea holds.
sections.code:
low addresses
+---------------------+
| text (code)         |  read-only, executable
| initialized data    |  globals/statics with values
| BSS                 |  zero-initialized globals/statics
| heap  ->            |  malloc / calloc / realloc
|        ...          |
|            <-  stack|  locals, args, return addresses
+---------------------+
high addresses

sections.heading: Text segment
bullets: Marked read-only so a stray write faults instead of corrupting code.
Shared between processes running the same program.

sections.heading: Initialized data segment
bullets: Global and static variables that have a non-zero initial value.
Stored in the executable file and loaded at start-up.
Lives for the whole program run.
sections.code:
int g = 10;            // initialized data
static int s = 20;     // initialized data

sections.heading: BSS segment
sections.body: BSS holds global and static variables with no initializer (or initialized to zero). The loader zero-fills it, so the executable only records its size, not its contents, which keeps binaries small.
sections.code:
int counter;           // BSS
static char buf[4096]; // BSS

sections.heading: Heap
bullets: Dynamic storage obtained with `malloc`, `calloc`, `realloc` and released with `free`.
Lifetime is controlled by the programmer, not by scope.

sections.heading: Stack
bullets: Each function call pushes a stack frame: arguments, return address, saved registers, and locals.
Frames are popped automatically on return.
Grows toward lower addresses on common architectures.
Deep recursion or huge local arrays cause stack overflow.

sections.body: The `size` tool reports text, data, and bss sizes of an executable. Adding an initialized global grows `data`; adding an uninitialized one grows `bss` only. Printing the address of a function, a global, a malloc result, and a local shows the ordering.

subtopics.title: Where do string literals and constants go?

sections.body: String literals typically live in a read-only data section, so writing through `char *s = "hi"; s[0] = 'H';` is undefined behavior. Use `char s[] = "hi";` to get a modifiable copy on the stack.

subtopics.title: Virtual memory view
subtopics.summary: Why addresses look the same in every process.

sections.body: Each process sees its own virtual address space; the OS and MMU map pages to physical frames. Segments are just regions of that virtual space with different permissions (r-x for text, rw- for data, heap, stack).
On Linux the object file groups bytes into sections (.text, .data, .bss, .rodata). The loader maps them into segments with permissions. `readelf -S` shows sections and `readelf -l` shows segments.

takeaways: Text is code (read-only); data/BSS hold globals; heap is manual; stack is automatic.
BSS costs no file space; it is zeroed at load.
Stack grows down, heap grows up on common platforms.
String literals are read-only: do not modify them.

references.label: Reference: Memory layout of C programs (GeeksforGeeks)

practice.title: Print the addresses of a global, static, local, and heap object and order them
Use the size command to see how initialized vs uninitialized globals change data and bss
Show stack growth direction with a recursive function
Explain why writing through a string literal pointer crashes
